opus-5.5.text:
I think it's actually been quite liberating. As you move into a faculty role and you're also involved in building a company, a lot of your time naturally goes into advising students, writing proposals, thinking about direction. For a while I worried that I'd slowly drift away from writing code myself, and for me that's always been an important part of how I think. A lot of my ideas, whether it was XGBoost or TVM or MLC, came from actually building things and running into problems with my own hands.

What AI coding tools do is lower the activation energy. Before, if I had a small idea, say I wanted to try a new scheduling trick or prototype a kernel variant, I'd need a solid block of a few hours just to set up the scaffolding, remember the APIs, write the boilerplate. With fragmented time, that often just didn't happen. Now I can sit down for thirty minutes, describe what I want, get a first draft, and spend my energy on the parts that really matter: the design decisions, the performance reasoning, checking whether the result is actually correct.

So in a sense the tools let me stay hands-on at the level I care about most. I still read the code carefully. In systems work, especially compilers and GPU kernels, small mistakes can be very subtle, so you can't just trust the output blindly. But the iteration loop is much faster, and that keeps me close to the engineering reality.

I also think it changes what being hands-on means. It's less about typing every line and more about being the person who understands the whole system, knows what to ask for, and can tell when something is wrong. That's always been the core skill anyway. The tools just remove some of the friction around it. And honestly, I find it a lot of fun. It brings back some of that feeling from my early days of hacking on projects, where you could just try things quickly and see what happens.

r001.rationale: The response says AI tools make prototyping and iteration easier, but it does not state that they make software refactoring substantially easier.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, I think it's one of the more interesting shifts of the last couple of years, and it's something I've been thinking about a lot personally.

For a long time, there's been this assumed trajectory in a research or engineering career: you start out writing a lot of code, and then as you take on more responsibility, you gradually drift away from it. You end up spending your time in meetings, writing documents, reviewing other people's work. And a lot of people feel a quiet loss there, because the hands-on part is what got them excited in the first place.

What AI tools have done, at least for me, is bend that curve back. The bottleneck for staying hands-on was never really understanding the problem. It was the sheer volume of mechanical work: wiring up a build, writing boilerplate, figuring out some unfamiliar API, chasing down a configuration issue. That stuff eats hours, and when you only have small fragments of time, those fragments get consumed before you reach anything interesting. Now I can describe what I want, get a reasonable scaffold back, and spend my limited time on the part that actually requires judgment: the design of an abstraction, whether a kernel is laid out correctly, where the performance is going.

So I find myself prototyping things again that I would have handed off before, simply because the activation energy is lower. That's valuable not just for personal satisfaction, but because you lose intuition when you stop touching the code. In systems work especially, in things like compilers or ML runtimes, a lot of the important decisions come from having felt the friction yourself.

At the same time, I'd push back on the idea that these tools replace the hands-on part. They change what hands-on means. Reviewing generated code carefully, understanding why something works, checking the edge cases: that's still very much engineering, and it demands more taste rather than less. The person who knows what good looks like gets a huge multiplier. The person who doesn't can generate a lot of plausible-looking code very quickly, which is a different kind of problem.

And there's an interesting feedback loop here for those of us who build ML systems. The tools that help me stay hands-on are themselves things we're trying to make faster and cheaper to run. So part of staying close to the code now is also staying close to how these models actually get deployed, and that feels like a pretty good place to be.

r001.rationale: The response says AI lowers the effort of scaffolding and prototyping, but it does not state that refactoring is substantially easier.

astra-6.text:
I think AI tools make it easier to stay hands-on because they reduce the effort needed to try an idea. If I’m working in an unfamiliar part of the stack, I can ask questions, get a first implementation, and start experimenting much faster.

But generating code is only part of software development. You still need to understand what problem you’re solving, whether the design makes sense, and how to check that it works. For me, the interesting possibility is spending less time on the mechanics and more time making those decisions. You can delegate some of the typing while staying very involved in the thinking.

r001.rationale: The candidate says AI tools make it easier to stay hands-on and speed up trying ideas, but it does not mention software refactoring or clearly say refactoring is substantially easier than without AI tools.

sol-6.1.text:
I think AI tools make it easier to stay hands-on, because they reduce the cost of trying an idea. If there’s a part of the codebase I’m less familiar with, I can ask questions, get a starting point, and move more quickly into experimenting.

But staying hands-on still means understanding what’s happening. You need to read the code, test it, and decide whether the approach makes sense. The tool can help you write something, but you still have to develop the judgment to know whether it’s the right thing to build.

So I see it as shortening the distance between an idea and an experiment. That can make development more engaging—you spend less time getting through the mechanical steps and more time exploring the actual problem.

r001.rationale: The response says AI makes experimentation and development easier, but it does not state that AI substantially eases software refactoring.
